misconceptions.statement: The fulcrum is the part of the lever where we hold and push.
misconceptions.why: Students link the fulcrum with the busy part where their hand acts rather than the still point.
misconceptions.fix: The fulcrum is the fixed point about which the lever turns. The hand applies effort at a different place.

probe.question: A crowbar lifts a stone with one end under the stone and your hands at the other end, resting on a brick. What is the fulcrum?
probe.wrong_answer: The end where my hands push.

misconceptions.root_belief: the part you act on is the pivot

misconceptions.statement: The fulcrum is always in the middle of the lever.
misconceptions.why: The see-saw, the most familiar lever, has its pivot at the centre.
misconceptions.fix: The fulcrum can be anywhere along the lever: in the middle, near the load or near the effort, depending on the class.

probe.question: In a wheelbarrow, where is the fulcrum?
probe.wrong_answer: In the middle of the wheelbarrow.

misconceptions.root_belief: one familiar example shows the general rule

misconceptions.statement: Effort is the heavy object that the lever moves.
misconceptions.why: Everyday use of 'effort' as trying hard gets mixed with the object being worked on.
misconceptions.fix: The load is the object or resistance that is moved. Effort is the force we apply to the lever.

probe.question: You press down on a spade handle to lift soil. What is the effort?
probe.wrong_answer: The soil that is being lifted.

misconceptions.root_belief: words from one context mean the same thing

misconceptions.statement: In a class 1 lever, the effort is always smaller than the load.
misconceptions.why: Students think every lever must make work easier by reducing force.
misconceptions.fix: In a class 1 lever, the effort can be smaller, equal or larger than the load, depending on how far each is from the fulcrum.

probe.question: A see-saw has a child sitting very close to the centre and a bigger child at the end. Is the effort of the first child smaller than the load?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, a class 1 lever always needs less effort.

misconceptions.root_belief: a tool always makes the job easier

misconceptions.statement: In a wheelbarrow, the handles are the fulcrum because we hold them.
misconceptions.why: Students think the part held in hand is the support point.
misconceptions.fix: In a wheelbarrow the wheel's axle is the fulcrum, the load is in the tray, and the effort is applied at the handles.

probe.question: Which part of a wheelbarrow is the fulcrum?
probe.wrong_answer: The handles.

misconceptions.root_belief: the part you hold is the pivot

misconceptions.statement: A class 3 lever always needs less effort than the load.
misconceptions.why: Students assume every lever gives a force advantage.
misconceptions.fix: In a class 3 lever the effort arm is shorter than the load arm, so more effort than load is needed. It gains speed and range of movement instead.

probe.question: Tweezers are used to pick up a small stone. Is the effort needed less than the weight of the stone?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, a lever reduces the effort.

misconceptions.root_belief: a tool always makes the job easier
misconceptions.source_hint: classroom studies on student ideas about simple machines and mechanical advantage

misconceptions.statement: In a pair of scissors, the paper being cut is the fulcrum.
misconceptions.why: Students pick the object in the middle of the action as the pivot.
misconceptions.fix: Scissors are two class 1 levers joined together. The screw or pivot joining the blades is the fulcrum, the paper is the load, and fingers give effort.

probe.question: What is the fulcrum of a pair of scissors?
probe.wrong_answer: The paper being cut.

misconceptions.root_belief: the object being acted on is the pivot

misconceptions.statement: A see-saw is not a lever because it keeps moving up and down.
misconceptions.why: Students picture levers as fixed tools like crowbars rather than playground equipment.
misconceptions.fix: A see-saw is a class 1 lever: a plank turning about a fixed middle point, with the children as load and effort.

probe.question: Is a see-saw a lever?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it is a playground toy that moves.

misconceptions.root_belief: a category is limited to its familiar examples

misconceptions.statement: Applying the effort closer to the fulcrum makes lifting the load easier.
misconceptions.why: Students think being near the pivot means more control and strength.
misconceptions.fix: The farther the effort is from the fulcrum, the longer the effort arm and the less effort is needed.

probe.question: To lift a heavy stone with a crowbar, where should you push to need the least effort?
probe.wrong_answer: Near the fulcrum, close to the stone.

misconceptions.root_belief: nearer to the action means more effect
misconceptions.source_hint: research on student reasoning about balance and torque on beams

misconceptions.statement: A see-saw balances only when the weights on both sides are equal.
misconceptions.why: Students attend only to weight and ignore distance from the fulcrum.
misconceptions.fix: A see-saw balances when load times its distance from the fulcrum equals effort times its distance. A lighter child sitting farther away can balance a heavier child.

probe.question: A 40 kg child sits far from the pivot and a 60 kg child sits close. Can the see-saw balance?
probe.wrong_answer: No, the 60 kg child will always go down because they are heavier.

misconceptions.root_belief: only one quantity decides the outcome
misconceptions.source_hint: research on children's ideas about balance beams

misconceptions.statement: A steeper ramp needs less effort because it is shorter.
misconceptions.why: Students think the shorter path is the easier path.
misconceptions.fix: A gentler slope needs less effort but the load has to travel a longer path. A steep ramp is shorter but needs more effort.

probe.question: To roll a drum onto a truck, which ramp needs less effort, a short steep one or a long gentle one?
probe.wrong_answer: The short steep one.

misconceptions.root_belief: the shorter path is the easier one

misconceptions.statement: Pushing a load up a ramp makes the load lighter.
misconceptions.why: The load feels easier to move, so students think its weight has changed.
misconceptions.fix: The weight of the load stays the same. The ramp lets us use a smaller force over a longer distance.

probe.question: A drum weighs 100 kg. What is its weight while it is being pushed up a ramp?
probe.wrong_answer: Less than 100 kg, as the ramp makes it lighter.

misconceptions.root_belief: the object changes, not how we handle it

misconceptions.statement: A fixed pulley reduces the effort needed to lift a load.
misconceptions.why: Students think any machine must reduce force, and pulling down feels easier with body weight.
misconceptions.fix: A fixed pulley only changes the direction of the effort. The effort needed equals the load.

probe.question: A 10 kg bucket is raised with one fixed pulley. How much effort is needed compared to its weight?
probe.wrong_answer: Less than the weight of the bucket.

misconceptions.root_belief: a tool always makes the job easier
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of student ideas about pulleys and mechanical advantage

misconceptions.statement: With a movable pulley, the rope end moves the same length as the load rises.
misconceptions.why: Students assume input and output distances are always equal.
misconceptions.fix: With a movable pulley, the rope must be pulled twice the distance the load rises, which is why the effort is halved.

probe.question: A load is raised 1 m using a movable pulley. How far must the rope end be pulled?

misconceptions.root_belief: input distance equals output distance
misconceptions.source_hint: research on students' reasoning about pulley systems

misconceptions.statement: A screwdriver with a thinner handle turns a screw more easily.
misconceptions.why: Students think smaller or finer tools need less force.
misconceptions.fix: A thicker handle has a larger radius, so the same turning effort is needed with less force. A thin handle needs more force.

probe.question: Which screwdriver turns a tight screw with less force: thick handle or thin handle?
probe.wrong_answer: The thin handle.

misconceptions.root_belief: smaller things need less force

misconceptions.statement: A wheel and axle means only the wheels of vehicles like carts.
misconceptions.why: The everyday word 'wheel' brings to mind vehicles.
misconceptions.fix: A wheel and axle is a large wheel fixed to a smaller axle. Door knobs, taps, steering wheels and screwdrivers also use it.

probe.question: Is a tap handle a wheel and axle machine?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it is not a vehicle wheel.

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

misconceptions.statement: Holding a heavy bag in your hands for a long time is a lot of work in science.
misconceptions.why: In daily language work means anything that tires you.
misconceptions.fix: In science, work is done only when a force moves an object in its direction. Holding a bag still involves no movement, so no work is done.

probe.question: A student holds a heavy bag without moving for 10 minutes. Is work done on the bag?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it is tiring.

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning
misconceptions.source_hint: research on everyday versus scientific meaning of work and energy

misconceptions.statement: A machine reduces the total work we have to do.
misconceptions.why: Students feel less effort and conclude that less work is done.
misconceptions.fix: A machine does not reduce work. It lets us use less force, but over a longer distance, so work stays about the same.

probe.question: A ramp lets you lift a box with half the effort. Is the work done less than lifting straight up?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, half the work.

misconceptions.root_belief: you can get more out than you put in
misconceptions.source_hint: studies on student ideas about machines and conservation of work

misconceptions.statement: A machine that needs less effort also makes the load move a shorter distance.
misconceptions.why: Students assume less force goes with less of everything.
misconceptions.fix: When a machine reduces effort, the effort has to move through a greater distance than the load moves.

probe.question: With a long crowbar, a small effort lifts a stone. Does the end you push move more or less than the stone?
probe.wrong_answer: Less than the stone.

misconceptions.root_belief: less of one thing means less of all

misconceptions.statement: A machine must have a motor or run on electricity.
misconceptions.why: Everyday machines like cars and washing machines are electrical or engine driven.
misconceptions.fix: A machine is any device that makes work easier by changing the size or direction of the force. Simple machines like levers and ramps need no power.

probe.question: Is a crowbar a machine?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it has no motor.

misconceptions.root_belief: only complicated things count as machines

misconceptions.statement: The class of a lever depends on its size or how strong it is.
misconceptions.why: Students use looks and size to categorise rather than the arrangement of fulcrum, load and effort.
misconceptions.fix: The class depends only on the order of fulcrum, load and effort along the lever, not on its size or material.

probe.question: A small nutcracker and a large wheelbarrow both have the load between the fulcrum and effort. Do they belong to the same class?
probe.wrong_answer: No, one is much bigger so it is in a different class.

misconceptions.root_belief: appearance decides the category

misconceptions.statement: A lever has to be a long straight stick.
misconceptions.why: Textbook pictures of levers mostly show straight rods and planks.
misconceptions.fix: A lever is any rigid bar that turns about a fixed point. Bent or short levers such as a claw hammer or a bottle opener also work as levers.

probe.question: Is a claw hammer pulling out a nail a lever?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it is bent, not a straight stick.

misconceptions.root_belief: a category is limited to its familiar examples
